title: Pressure-cooker lamb shanks
subtitle: Fork-tender in 45 minutes instead of three hours
excerpt: Lamb shanks braised in red wine and tomatoes under pressure. The meat falls from the bone in under an hour; the sauce reduces to a rich gravy while you make the mash.
sourceNotes: Braised lamb shanks are a fixture of Mediterranean and British winter cooking. The combination of red wine, rosemary, and tomatoes follows the method seen in River Cafe Cook Book (Rogers and Gray, 1995) and Simon Hopkinson's Roast Chicken and Other Stories (1994).

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely, transfer shanks and sauce to airtight containers, and freeze for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat gently with a splash of stock.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dish improves significantly overnight. Reheat the shanks covered in the sauce, low and slow, on the hob.

content.text: Lamb shanks are the ideal pressure-cooker cut, a working muscle with enough collagen to break down into a rich, silky sauce, but one that would take 2 to 3 hours in the oven. Under high pressure, the same result comes in 45 minutes. The shank meat should fall away from the bone without prompting when you prod it.

Brown the shanks in a separate frying pan first. The pressure cooker base is too narrow to get a proper sear on four shanks without steaming them. A hot, wide pan and a few minutes per side is worth the extra washing up.
Serve with mashed potato or soft polenta, which will hold the sauce. The braising liquid reduces to a coating consistency in the same amount of time it takes to make the mash.

Season the lamb shanks all over with salt and pepper. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large frying pan over high heat. Sear the shanks in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, until dark brown on all surfaces. Transfer to the pressure cooker.

Reduce the heat in the frying pan to medium. Add the onion and carrot and cook for 4 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and tomato puree; stir for 1 minute. Pour in {{red-wine}} of red wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping up any browned bits. Pour this over the shanks in the pressure cooker.

Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, the tinned tomatoes, and the rosemary sprigs to the pressure cooker. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 45 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of at least 15 minutes before opening.

Lift the shanks out carefully, they will be fragile. Strain the braising liquid into a wide saucepan. Bring to a brisk boil and reduce for 8 to 10 minutes until the sauce coats the back of a spoon. Return the shanks to warm through. Discard the rosemary.

rows.symptom: The meat is not falling from the bone
rows.cause: The shanks were particularly large, or the pressure cooker did not reach full pressure during cooking.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 10 to 15 minutes. Lamb shanks cannot really overcook into dryness at this stage, only into greater tenderness.

rows.cause: The braising liquid was not reduced after opening.
rows.fix: Transfer the sauce to a wide saucepan and boil over high heat for 10 to 15 minutes until it thickens and coats the back of a spoon.

rows.symptom: The meat looks dry but the sauce is rich
rows.cause: The shanks sat above the liquid level during cooking.
rows.fix: Next time, ensure the liquid reaches at least halfway up the shanks. The problem is cosmetic, the meat underneath the surface will be tender. Serve the shanks covered with sauce.

rows.cause: The wine was not cooked down enough before adding to the pot, or the tinned tomatoes were sharp.
rows.fix: Add a pinch of sugar or a small knob of butter stirred through the sauce to round the acidity.

content.text: The dish improves with a night in the fridge, the fat solidifies and can be lifted off, and the flavours deepen. Reheat the shanks covered in the sauce over low heat on the hob. To freeze, cool completely, portion with enough sauce to cover, and freeze for up to 3 months.

Braised lamb shanks became a fixture of restaurant menus in the 1990s before settling into the home-cooking repertoire. They suit a Sunday or a dinner party, a dish that looks and tastes like work but, with the pressure cooker, is mostly waiting. Pair with the best mashed potato you can make and a green vegetable on the side.
